::: {.callout-note}
## How this project works
Every search result this report uses is stored in the folder `data/`. The
**first** render sends the searches to OpenAlex, Crossref, EconBiz and EconStor
and saves each answer there. This will already been done once you look at this
file. **Every later render reads the saved answers** and
sends no request at all -- and that includes *you* first run.
That makes the report reproducible: you get exactly the
numbers in this report, even though the databases keep changing — and you need
no API key to reproduce it.

To run the searches again with today's data, render with
`quarto render report.qmd -P refresh:true`. This needs your own OpenAlex API
key (see the setup below) and overwrites the saved answers.
:::

# Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
here::i_am("report.qmd")

# Searches with Umlauten (Arbeitszeitverkürzung) need a UTF-8 session: in the
# "C" locale, which R gets when started from some terminals, the umlaut is
# sent as the text "<c3><bc>" and silently matches nothing. RStudio and
# Windows use UTF-8 by default.
if (!l10n_info()$`UTF-8`) invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))

library(here)
library(openalexR)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(flextable)
library(httr2)
library(xml2)

# OpenAlex needs a free API key for searches: store it in your user-level
# .Renviron as OPENALEX_KEY=... (usethis::edit_r_environ() opens the file).
# It is only used when a saved answer is missing or refresh = true.
options(openalexR.apikey = Sys.getenv("OPENALEX_KEY"))

dir.create(here("data"), showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

Two helpers give all tables and figures the same look: `nice_table()` turns a
data frame into a formatted table, `theme_review()` is the ggplot2 theme.

```{r}
#| label: style
euf_blue <- "#00395B"
euf_grey <- "#6F6F6F"

set_flextable_defaults(font.size = 10, padding = 4, big.mark = ",")

nice_table <- function(df) {
  ft <- df |>
    flextable() |>
    theme_booktabs() |>
    bold(part = "header") |>
    color(color = euf_blue, part = "header")
  years <- intersect(names(df), "Year") # years without a thousands separator
  if (length(years)) ft <- colformat_int(ft, j = years, big.mark = "")
  autofit(ft)
}

theme_review <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor    = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x  = element_blank(),
      axis.title          = element_text(colour = euf_grey),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
}
theme_set(theme_review())
```

The helper `cached()` is what makes the report reproducible. It returns the
saved answer from `data/` if there is one. Only if there isn't does it run the
search, save the answer, and note the date in `data/retrieval_log.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: cached
cached <- function(name, expr, needs_key = FALSE) {
  file <- here("data", str_c(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(file) && !isTRUE(params$refresh)) {
    return(read_rds(file))
  }
  if (needs_key && !nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENALEX_KEY"))) {
    stop("data/", name, ".rds is missing and no OPENALEX_KEY is set. ",
         "Add your OpenAlex key to ~/.Renviron and restart R.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  value <- expr # the search runs only here (lazy evaluation)
  write_rds(value, file)

  log_file <- here("data", "retrieval_log.csv")
  log <- if (file.exists(log_file)) {
    read_csv(log_file, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
  } else {
    tibble(object = character(), retrieved = character(), rows = character())
  }
  log |>
    filter(object != name) |>
    bind_rows(tibble(object = name,
                     retrieved = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z"),
                     rows = as.character(NROW(value)))) |>
    write_csv(log_file)
  value
}

clean_doi <- function(x) str_to_lower(str_remove(x, "^https://doi.org/"))
short_id  <- function(x) str_remove(x, ".*/")
```

@tbl-retrieval shows when each saved answer was retrieved. These are the
dates to report for the searches.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-retrieval
#| tbl-cap: "When each saved search result was retrieved."
log_file <- here("data", "retrieval_log.csv")
if (file.exists(log_file)) {
  read_csv(log_file, col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |>
    rename(`Saved result` = object, Retrieved = retrieved, Rows = rows) |>
    nice_table()
}
```

# Step 3: the search in OpenAlex

The string is the one from the tutorial, built from its concept table. It is
written exactly as in the web interface. Note that the API uses commas to separate
filters, so the string contains none.

```{r}
#| label: query
query <- '("four-day week" OR "four day week" OR "4-day week"
  OR "four-day workweek" OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
  OR "reduced working hours" OR "reduction in working hours"
  OR "shorter working week" OR "shorter workweek")
  AND (productivity OR productive OR "well-being" OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absenteeism OR turnover OR performance)'
query <- str_squish(query) # one line, single spaces
```

First only the number of hits — cheap, and enough to compare string versions:

```{r}
#| label: count
n_hits <- cached("openalex_count", needs_key = TRUE, oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = query,
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en",
  count_only = TRUE
))
n_hits$count
```

See how OpenAlex reads the string and note the `stemmed` before each term:
stemming is switched on automatically.

```{r}
#| label: oql
n_hits$x_query$oql
```

Then the records themselves:

```{r}
#| label: fetch
works <- cached("openalex_works", needs_key = TRUE, oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = query,
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en"
))
```

The search returns `r nrow(works)` articles and reviews in English.

## The test set

Four papers that a good search should find (@tbl-test-set). Two are
closed-access articles from Elsevier journals, for which OpenAlex has no
abstract — exactly the records that a title-and-abstract search can only find
through their titles.

```{r}
#| label: test-set
test_set <- tibble(
  paper = c("Lepinteur, Labour Economics",
            "Mullens & Laurijssen, BMC Public Health",
            "Raposo & van Ours, Economics Letters",
            "Nord & Costigan, Journal of Applied Psychology"),
  doi = c("10.1016/j.labeco.2018.05.010",
          "10.1186/s12889-024-19161-x",
          "10.1016/j.econlet.2009.10.001",
          "10.1037/h0035419")
)

# The test-set records themselves: titles, and do they have an abstract?
test_records <- cached("openalex_test_set", needs_key = TRUE,
                       oa_fetch(entity = "works", doi = test_set$doi)) |>
  mutate(doi = clean_doi(doi))

test_set <- test_set |>
  left_join(test_records |> select(doi, title, abstract), by = "doi") |>
  mutate(found_by_string = doi %in% clean_doi(works$doi),
         has_abstract    = !is.na(abstract) & abstract != "") |>
  select(-abstract)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-set
#| tbl-cap: "The test set: is each paper found by the string, and does OpenAlex have its abstract?"
test_set |>
  transmute(Paper = paper, Title = title,
            `Abstract in OpenAlex` = if_else(has_abstract, "yes", "no"),
            `Found by the string` = if_else(found_by_string, "yes", "no")) |>
  nice_table() |>
  width(j = "Title", width = 3)
```

The string finds `r sum(test_set$found_by_string)` of the
`r nrow(test_set)` test papers. The pattern is the one the lecture predicts:

- Both papers **with an abstract** in OpenAlex are found.
- Of the papers **without an abstract**, only titles can match, so they are
  found only if their title contains a term from *both* concepts. Lepinteur's
  title ("The shorter workweek and worker wellbeing") does. Raposo & van
  Ours ("How working time reduction affects jobs and wages") names the
  intervention but not an outcome from our list; Nord & Costigan ("Worker
  adjustment to the four-day week") names the intervention, but "adjustment"
  is not in the outcome block either.

Two responses are possible, and both are legitimate if documented. Widen the
outcome block (e.g. with *employment*, *wages*, *adjustment*) — at the cost of
precision — or accept the miss and rely on snowballing (step 6) to find papers
like these. Whatever you choose goes into the search log.

## The abstract gap

How many of the hits have no abstract — and where are they concentrated?

```{r}
#| label: abstract-gap
works <- works |>
  mutate(no_abstract = is.na(abstract) | abstract == "")

gap <- works |>
  summarise(records = n(), without = sum(no_abstract), share = mean(no_abstract))

gap_publisher <- works |>
  mutate(publisher = coalesce(host_organization_name, "(no publisher recorded)")) |>
  group_by(publisher) |>
  summarise(records = n(), without = sum(no_abstract)) |>
  arrange(desc(records))

gap_big_two <- gap_publisher |>
  filter(str_detect(publisher, "Elsevier|Springer")) |>
  summarise(without = sum(without)) |>
  pull(without)
```

Of the `r gap$records` records, `r gap$without`
(`r scales::percent(gap$share)`) have no abstract in OpenAlex.
@tbl-gap-publisher shows where they come from.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gap-publisher
#| tbl-cap: "Records and records without abstract, for the ten publishers with the most records."
gap_publisher |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(share = scales::percent(without / records, accuracy = 1)) |>
  rename(Publisher = publisher, Records = records,
         `Without abstract` = without, Share = share) |>
  nice_table()
```

Two things in @tbl-gap-publisher need a comment:

- **The largest group has no publisher at all.** This is not an error in the
  code. OpenAlex knows a publisher only for sources it has matched to one;
  small, regional or new journals, repositories and records without any source
  have none. Note that this group hardly ever lacks an abstract: these are
  mostly open outlets that pass their abstracts on to OpenAlex.
- **The gap sits with two publishers.** Elsevier and Springer Nature account
  for `r gap_big_two` of the `r gap$without` records without abstract — the
  abstract takedowns discussed in the lecture.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap-period
#| fig-cap: "Share of hits without an abstract in OpenAlex, by publication period. Numbers above the bars: share and number of records."
gap_period <- works |>
  mutate(period = cut(publication_year, c(-Inf, 1999, 2009, 2019, Inf),
                      labels = c("before 2000", "2000–2009", "2010–2019", "since 2020"))) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(records = n(), share = mean(no_abstract))

ggplot(gap_period, aes(x = period, y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = euf_blue, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = str_c(scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1),
                              "\n(n = ", records, ")")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5, colour = euf_grey) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Records without abstract")
```

@fig-gap-period shows that the gap is smallest for the most recent records,
which are more often open access. Keep in mind that all these shares
*understate* the problem: a record without an abstract can only be found
through its title, so such records are under-represented among the hits to
begin with. These numbers belong in the limitations paragraph.

## The result set

```{r}
#| label: fig-years
#| fig-cap: "Hits per publication year."
works |>
  count(publication_year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = publication_year, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = euf_blue, width = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Records")
```

Most hits are recent (@fig-years): `r sum(works$publication_year >= 2020)` of
`r nrow(works)` are from 2020 or later, reflecting both the recent debate on
the four-day week and the general growth of publishing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "The ten most frequent sources of the hits."
works |>
  mutate(source = coalesce(source_display_name, "(no source recorded)")) |>
  count(source, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10) |>
  rename(Source = source, Records = n) |>
  nice_table()
```

@tbl-sources needs a careful reading:

- **No source recorded** is again a gap in the metadata, not in the code: for
  these records OpenAlex knows a title and a year, but not where the work
  appeared.
- **Zenodo is not a journal** but a repository where anyone can upload
  documents. OpenAlex treats repositories, preprint servers and PubMed as
  "sources", and it classifies many uploads as articles — so the filter
  `type = "article"` does not guarantee a peer-reviewed journal article. That
  is a screening decision, and it belongs in your criteria.
- **The hits are scattered**: the `r nrow(works)` records come from
  `r n_distinct(works$source_display_name, na.rm = TRUE)` different sources,
  and no source contributes more than a handful. Some come from medicine
  (rheumatology, health economics), where "productivity" means the work
  productivity lost to an illness — a first sign that the outcome block costs
  precision.

## Two strings, two vocabularies

Terminology bias becomes visible when strings built from different
vocabularies are compared. String A uses only the "four-day week" terms. The
full string adds "working time reduction" and related terms.

```{r}
#| label: compare-strings
string_a <- '("four-day week" OR "four day week" OR "4-day week")
  AND (productivity OR productive OR "well-being" OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absenteeism OR turnover OR performance)'

works_a <- cached("openalex_string_a", needs_key = TRUE, oa_fetch(
  entity = "works",
  title_and_abstract.search = str_squish(string_a),
  type = c("article", "review"),
  language = "en"
))

only_full <- setdiff(works$id, works_a$id)
only_a    <- setdiff(works_a$id, works$id)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-strings
#| tbl-cap: "Hits of the two strings."
tibble(
  `String A: four-day week terms only` = nrow(works_a),
  `Full string` = nrow(works),
  `Only the full string` = length(only_full),
  `Only string A` = length(only_a)
) |>
  nice_table()
```

The "four-day week" vocabulary alone finds only a small fraction of the
records (@tbl-strings). Most of the literature speaks of *working time
reduction* or *reduced working hours* — a review built on the popular term
would have missed most of it. @tbl-only-full shows a sample of what only the
full string finds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-only-full
#| tbl-cap: "The five most-cited records that only the full string finds."
works |>
  filter(id %in% only_full) |>
  slice_max(cited_by_count, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Year = publication_year, Title = title,
            Source = coalesce(source_display_name, "(none)")) |>
  nice_table() |>
  width(j = "Title", width = 3.5)
```

A handful of records appear only under string A, although the full string
contains all its terms. They are off-topic, and the reason lies in the search
engine rather than in the logic of the strings — a reminder to look at such
cases by hand instead of trusting Boolean logic blindly.

# Step 5: the screening sheet

One row per record, records without an abstract first. The sheet is written
to `output/` and rebuilt on every render.

```{r}
#| label: screening-sheet
screening <- works |>
  transmute(id, doi, publication_year, title, source_display_name, abstract,
            abstract_source = if_else(no_abstract, "", "OpenAlex"))
```

## Fill in abstracts from Crossref

Some publishers deposit abstracts with Crossref, the DOI registration agency.
Elsevier and Springer Nature do not, so their abstracts still have to be
copied from the publisher page by hand.

```{r}
#| label: crossref
crossref_abstract <- function(doi) {
  res <- tryCatch(
    request(str_c("https://api.crossref.org/works/", doi)) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json(),
    error = function(e) NULL # no record or no access: NULL
  )
  ab <- res$message$abstract
  if (is.null(ab)) NA_character_ else str_squish(str_remove_all(ab, "<[^>]+>"))
}

missing_dois <- screening |>
  filter(abstract_source == "", !is.na(doi)) |>
  pull(doi) |>
  clean_doi()

crossref <- cached("crossref_abstracts", tibble(
  doi = missing_dois,
  crossref = map_chr(missing_dois, \(d) {
    Sys.sleep(0.2) # be polite to the API
    crossref_abstract(d)
  })
))

screening <- screening |>
  mutate(doi_clean = clean_doi(doi)) |>
  left_join(crossref, by = c("doi_clean" = "doi")) |>
  mutate(
    abstract_source = if_else(!is.na(crossref), "Crossref", abstract_source),
    abstract = coalesce(crossref, abstract)
  ) |>
  select(-doi_clean, -crossref)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-abstract-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Where the abstracts in the screening sheet come from."
screening |>
  count(Source = if_else(abstract_source == "", "still missing", abstract_source)) |>
  rename(Records = n) |>
  nice_table()
```

Crossref fills in `r sum(!is.na(crossref$crossref))` of the
`r nrow(crossref)` missing abstracts (@tbl-abstract-sources). That is not a
failure of the code: the records without abstract are almost all from
Elsevier and Springer Nature, and these publishers deposit no abstracts with
Crossref either. For them, the only route is the publisher's page — by hand,
recording "publisher page" in `abstract_source`.

```{r}
#| label: write-sheet
screening |>
  mutate(decision_ta = "", reason_ta = "", decision_ft = "",
         reason_ft = "", notes = "") |>
  arrange(abstract_source) |> # records without abstract first
  write_excel_csv(here("output", "screening_sheet.csv"))
```

The decisions are recorded in `data/screening_decisions.csv` (columns `id`,
`decision_ta`, `reason_ta`, `decision_ft`, `reason_ft`, `screener`, `notes`);
the section "Screening the records" below reports them, and the flow diagram
in step 8 is drawn from them.

# Step 6: snowballing

Snowballing collects, for a few seed papers, the papers they cite (backward)
and the papers that cite them (forward). Which seeds you choose decides what
you get — as the two runs below show.

## First run: seeds chosen by citation count

A tempting shortcut is to take the most-cited hits as seeds:

```{r}
#| label: snowball-cited
seeds_cited <- works |> slice_max(cited_by_count, n = 2, with_ties = FALSE)

snow_cited <- cached("openalex_snowball", needs_key = TRUE,
                     oa_snowball(identifier = short_id(seeds_cited$id)))

# Links from a seed point backward (to its references), links to a seed
# point forward (from papers citing it)
links_cited <- snow_cited$edges |>
  mutate(direction = if_else(from %in% short_id(seeds_cited$id),
                             "backward", "forward")) |>
  count(direction)

new_cited <- snow_cited$nodes |>
  filter(!oa_input, !short_id(id) %in% short_id(works$id))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-seeds-cited
#| tbl-cap: "Seeds chosen by citation count: the two most-cited hits."
seeds_cited |>
  transmute(Year = publication_year, Title = title, Citations = cited_by_count) |>
  nice_table() |>
  width(j = "Title", width = 4)
```

The result is a lesson in itself. The most-cited hit (@tbl-seeds-cited) is
about the economic burden of dementia: it matched the string through generic
words such as "productivity", and it is cited mainly by medical research.
Snowballing from it returns `r nrow(new_cited)` new records — most of them
forward citations
(`r links_cited |> filter(direction == "forward") |> pull(n)` forward against
`r links_cited |> filter(direction == "backward") |> pull(n)` backward links) —
and almost none of them on working time. Most cited is not most relevant:
seeds must be *included* papers, chosen for their fit with the question.

## Second run: seeds chosen for their fit

The second run uses the two test-set papers that the string found and that
fit the question best:

```{r}
#| label: snowball-fit
seeds_fit <- works |>
  filter(clean_doi(doi) %in% test_set$doi[test_set$found_by_string])

snow_fit <- cached("openalex_snowball_fit", needs_key = TRUE,
                   oa_snowball(identifier = short_id(seeds_fit$id)))

candidates_fit <- snow_fit$nodes |> filter(!oa_input)
new_fit <- candidates_fit |>
  filter(!short_id(id) %in% short_id(works$id))
```

Even from good seeds, snowballing returns more records than one would want to
screen by hand. A documented, reproducible way to narrow them down is a
**title filter**: keep only the new records whose title mentions working time
at all. It is a coarse screening step — and, like every screening step, it is
reported: in the flow diagram, the filtered-out records are the difference
between the records identified and the reports sought in the snowballing arm.

```{r}
#| label: title-filter
time_terms <- regex(
  "four[- ]day|4[- ]day|working[- ]time|work[- ]time|working hours|work hours|hours of work|workweek|work week|working week",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)
new_fit_filtered <- new_fit |>
  filter(str_detect(coalesce(title, ""), time_terms))

# Sheet for screening the snowballed records by hand
new_fit_filtered |>
  transmute(id, doi, publication_year, title, source_display_name, abstract,
            decision_ft = "", reason_ft = "", notes = "") |>
  write_excel_csv(here("output", "snowball_sheet.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-snowball
#| tbl-cap: "The two snowballing runs compared."
tibble(
  Run = c("Seeds by citation count", "Seeds chosen for fit"),
  `Records linked to the seeds` = c(nrow(snow_cited$nodes |> filter(!oa_input)),
                                    nrow(candidates_fit)),
  `New (not found by the string)` = c(nrow(new_cited), nrow(new_fit)),
  `New, after the title filter` = c(
    sum(str_detect(coalesce(new_cited$title, ""), time_terms)),
    nrow(new_fit_filtered)),
  `Test papers found` = c(
    sum(test_set$doi %in% clean_doi(snow_cited$nodes$doi)),
    sum(test_set$doi %in% clean_doi(snow_fit$nodes$doi)))
) |>
  nice_table()
```

@tbl-snowball compares the two runs. With well-chosen seeds, snowballing
does what it is for: it reaches papers that the string missed. Lepinteur's
reference list, for instance, contains Raposo & van Ours — one of the two
test papers the string could not find, because OpenAlex has no abstract for
it. @tbl-snowball-test shows which test papers each route finds.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-snowball-test
#| tbl-cap: "Which route finds which test paper?"
test_set |>
  transmute(
    Paper = paper,
    `String` = if_else(found_by_string, "yes", "no"),
    `Snowballing (seeds by citations)` =
      if_else(doi %in% clean_doi(snow_cited$nodes$doi), "yes", "no"),
    `Snowballing (seeds by fit)` =
      if_else(doi %in% clean_doi(snow_fit$nodes$doi), "yes", "no")
  ) |>
  nice_table()
```

The new records that pass the title filter are written to
`output/snowball_sheet.csv` and screened with the same criteria; the
decisions are in `data/snowball_decisions.csv`.

# Screening the records

::: {.callout-warning}
## Disclosure about screening
The decisions in `data/screening_decisions.csv` and
`data/snowball_decisions.csv` were made by an **AI assistant (Claude)**, as a
demonstration for this tutorial, and have **not been checked by myself**.
In a real review this would have to be disclosed exactly like this, and a
person would have to check at least a sample of the decisions — the lecture
explains why. Two further limitations follow from it:

- The second round is based on the **abstracts**, read against the criteria
  more strictly than in round 1; the full texts were not consulted.
- Where neither title nor abstract allowed a decision, the record counts as
  **not retrievable**.
- I did this because I currently do not have the ressources to complete the 
  screening myself, and this is a tutorial for illustration. Do not do it like
  this in situations that matter more, such as an exam or a thesis.
:::

The criteria are those of the tutorial (step 1):

- **Include:** empirical studies, quantitative or qualitative, of an *actual*
  reduction in working time — at firm, sector or country level — that report
  at least one outcome for employees or firms.
- **Exclude:** conceptual and normative papers, models and simulations;
  reviews; compressed work weeks (the same hours in fewer days), preferences
  for a hypothetical reduction, cross-sectional comparisons of hours and
  individually chosen part-time work; studies without an outcome for
  employees or firms; papers not in English.

Round 1 (titles and abstracts) excluded what was clearly out; round 2 applied
the criteria strictly and records one reason from a fixed list for every
exclusion.

```{r}
#| label: decisions
read_decisions <- function(f) read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

screened <- read_decisions(here("data", "screening_decisions.csv")) |>
  filter(id %in% works$id)
snowball <- read_decisions(here("data", "snowball_decisions.csv")) |>
  filter(id %in% new_fit_filtered$id)

# Empty cells are read as NA: filter() drops them, so these ID lists are clean
included_db_ids   <- screened |> filter(decision_ft == "include") |> pull(id)
included_snow_ids <- snowball |> filter(decision_ft == "include") |> pull(id)

n_dup      <- screened |> filter(reason_ta == "Duplicate") |> nrow()
n_kept     <- sum(screened$decision_ta == "include")
n_included <- length(included_db_ids)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-round1
#| tbl-cap: "Round 1 (titles and abstracts) of the database records."
screened |>
  mutate(Decision = if_else(decision_ta == "include", "kept for round 2",
                            str_c("excluded: ", reason_ta))) |>
  count(Decision, sort = TRUE) |>
  rename(Records = n) |>
  nice_table()
```

Of the `r nrow(screened)` records, `r n_dup` are duplicates, and only
`r n_kept` survive round 1 (@tbl-round1). Most of the others are off-topic:
"productivity", "performance", "stress" or "satisfaction" combined with some
mention of working hours occur everywhere in medicine and engineering. This
is the low precision that @tbl-sources already hinted at.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-round2
#| tbl-cap: "Round 2: decisions and exclusion reasons, for the database records and the snowballed records."
bind_rows(
  screened |> filter(decision_ta == "include") |> mutate(Arm = "Database"),
  snowball |> mutate(Arm = "Snowballing")
) |>
  mutate(Decision = case_when(decision_ft == "include" ~ "included",
                              decision_ft == "not retrievable" ~ "not retrievable",
                              TRUE ~ str_c("excluded: ", reason_ft))) |>
  count(Arm, Decision) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Arm, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(desc(Database)) |>
  nice_table()
```

The most frequent exclusion reason in round 2 (@tbl-round2) is that a study
does not look at a reduction in working time. Many studies from the 1970s
examine a "four-day week" that was in fact a *compressed* week of four
ten-hour days — exactly the terminology trap that step 1 of the tutorial warns
about. Others compare people who happen to work fewer hours, or ask about
preferences for a reduction that has not happened.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-included
#| tbl-cap: "The test set after screening."
test_set |>
  left_join(works |> transmute(id, doi = clean_doi(doi)), by = "doi") |>
  left_join(snow_fit$nodes |> transmute(id_snow = id, doi = clean_doi(doi)),
            by = "doi") |>
  mutate(
    Route = case_when(found_by_string ~ "string",
                      !is.na(id_snow) ~ "snowballing",
                      TRUE ~ "not found"),
    Included = case_when(
      !is.na(id) & id %in% included_db_ids ~ "yes",
      !is.na(id_snow) & short_id(id_snow) %in% short_id(included_snow_ids) ~ "yes",
      TRUE ~ "no")
  ) |>
  transmute(Paper = paper, `Found by` = Route, Included) |>
  distinct() |>
  nice_table()
```

Three of the four test papers end up in the review (@tbl-test-included) —
one of them only thanks to snowballing. The fourth, a 1973 study without an
abstract whose title lacks every outcome term, is found by neither route: a
residual gap of the kind the limitations paragraph has to name.

# Digression: a second database — EconBiz

EconBiz needs no key. The helper puts the same terms into the title, abstract
and description fields, because abstracts sit in one of the last two,
depending on the source.

```{r}
#| label: econbiz-query
in_fields <- function(terms, fields = c("title", "abstract", "description")) {
  str_c("(", str_c(fields, ":(", terms, ")", collapse = " OR "), ")")
}
work_terms <- '"four-day week" OR "4-day week" OR "four day week"
  OR "working time reduction" OR "work time reduction"
  OR "reduced working hours" OR "shorter working week"'
outcome_terms <- 'productiv* OR well-being OR wellbeing OR satisfaction
  OR burnout OR stress OR absentee* OR turnover OR performance'
eb_query <- str_squish(
  str_c(in_fields(work_terms), " AND ", in_fields(outcome_terms))
)
```

`from` counts from 1; a fixed sort order (`id asc`) makes the pages fit
together.

```{r}
#| label: econbiz-search
econbiz_search <- function(q, page_size = 500) {
  fetch <- function(from) {
    request("https://api.econbiz.de/v1/search") |>
      req_url_query(q = q, size = page_size, from = from, sort = "id asc") |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()
  }
  first <- fetch(1)
  hits  <- first$hits$hits
  while (length(hits) < first$hits$total) {
    page <- fetch(length(hits) + 1)$hits$hits
    if (length(page) == 0) break
    hits <- c(hits, page)
  }
  first_or_na <- function(x) if (length(x)) as.character(x[[1]]) else NA_character_
  map(hits, \(x) {
    urls <- unlist(x$identifier_url)
    tibble(
      id     = x$id,
      source = first_or_na(x$source),
      type   = first_or_na(x$type),
      year   = as.integer(str_extract(first_or_na(x$date), "[0-9]{4}")),
      title  = first_or_na(x$title),
      doi    = first_or_na(str_to_lower(str_remove(
                 str_subset(urls, "doi.org/"), ".*doi.org/"))),
      handle = first_or_na(str_extract(urls, "10419/[0-9]+") |> discard(is.na))
    )
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

eb_raw <- cached("econbiz_en", econbiz_search(eb_query))
```

Drop events, then duplicates within EconBiz — first by DOI, then by title and
year:

```{r}
#| label: econbiz-clean
eb <- eb_raw |>
  filter(type != "event") |>
  mutate(title_key = str_to_lower(str_remove_all(title, "[^[:alnum:]]"))) |>
  filter(is.na(doi) | !duplicated(doi)) |>
  distinct(title_key, year, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

Of the `r nrow(eb_raw)` EconBiz records, `r nrow(eb)` remain after removing
events and duplicates. @tbl-econbiz-sources shows where they come from.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-econbiz-sources
#| tbl-cap: "EconBiz records after cleaning, by source and type of publication."
eb |>
  count(source, type, sort = TRUE) |>
  rename(Source = source, Type = type, Records = n) |>
  nice_table()
```

EconBiz is strong where OpenAlex is weak: books from the ZBW catalogue
(ECONIS), working papers (RePEc, EconStor) and reports — the kind of
literature that a database of journal articles under-represents.

Abstracts for records in EconStor, via its OAI-PMH interface:

```{r}
#| label: econstor
econstor_abstract <- function(handle) {
  oai <- request("https://www.econstor.eu/oai/request") |>
    req_url_query(verb = "GetRecord", metadataPrefix = "oai_dc",
                  identifier = str_c("oai:econstor.eu:", handle)) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_xml()
  abstract <- xml_find_first(oai, ".//dc:description", xml_ns(oai))
  if (inherits(abstract, "xml_missing")) NA_character_ else xml_text(abstract)
}

handles <- eb |> filter(!is.na(handle)) |> distinct(handle) |> pull(handle)
econstor <- cached("econstor_abstracts", tibble(
  handle = handles,
  abstract = map_chr(handles, \(h) {
    Sys.sleep(0.5) # be polite
    tryCatch(econstor_abstract(h), error = function(e) NA_character_)
  })
))

eb <- eb |> left_join(econstor, by = "handle")
```

EconStor provides abstracts for `r sum(!is.na(eb$abstract))` of the
`r nrow(eb)` records; for the others, the DOI or the catalogue entry leads to
the abstract.

```{r}
#| label: econbiz-compare
oa_dois <- works |> filter(!is.na(doi)) |> pull(doi) |> clean_doi() |> unique()
eb_dois <- eb |> filter(!is.na(doi)) |> pull(doi) |> unique()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-econbiz-compare
#| tbl-cap: "OpenAlex and EconBiz compared by DOI."
tibble(
  `Only OpenAlex` = length(setdiff(oa_dois, eb_dois)),
  `Only EconBiz` = length(setdiff(eb_dois, oa_dois)),
  Both = length(intersect(oa_dois, eb_dois)),
  `EconBiz without DOI` = sum(is.na(eb$doi))
) |>
  nice_table()
```

The overlap is small (@tbl-econbiz-compare), but read it with care: fewer
than half of the EconBiz records have a DOI at all, and books and working
papers rarely do. A comparison by DOI therefore understates the overlap — and
the EconBiz records without DOI are exactly the books and working papers that
OpenAlex is weakest on.

The German-language literature, which the English-only OpenAlex search
excludes:

```{r}
#| label: econbiz-german
de_terms <- 'Arbeitszeitverkürzung OR "Vier-Tage-Woche" OR "4-Tage-Woche"'
eb_de <- cached("econbiz_de", econbiz_search(in_fields(de_terms)))
```

The German search finds `r nrow(eb_de)` records in EconBiz — more than the
English OpenAlex search finds in total. Restricting a review to English is a
legitimate choice, but on this topic it is a consequential one, and it belongs
in the limitations.

# Step 8: the flow diagram

```{r}
#| label: prisma-data
library(PRISMA2020)

template <- read_csv(system.file("extdata", "PRISMA.csv", package = "PRISMA2020"),
                     col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
set_n <- function(tab, field, value) {
  if (!field %in% tab$data) stop("Unknown box in PRISMA template: ", field)
  tab |> mutate(n = if_else(data == field, as.character(value), n))
}
# PRISMA2020 expects "reason, n; reason, n" -- so the reasons themselves must
# not contain a comma or a semicolon
reasons_text <- function(d) {
  r <- d |> filter(decision_ft == "exclude") |> count(reason_ft, sort = TRUE)
  stopifnot(!any(str_detect(r$reason_ft, "[,;]")))
  str_c(r$reason_ft, ", ", r$n, collapse = "; ")
}

sought        <- screened |> filter(decision_ta == "include") |> nrow()
not_retrieved <- screened |> filter(decision_ft == "not retrievable") |> nrow()
included_snow <- length(included_snow_ids)

counts <- list(
  database_results           = nrow(works),
  duplicates                 = n_dup,
  records_screened           = nrow(works) - n_dup,
  records_excluded           = nrow(works) - n_dup - sought,
  dbr_sought_reports         = sought,
  dbr_notretrieved_reports   = not_retrieved,
  dbr_assessed               = sought - not_retrieved,
  dbr_excluded               = reasons_text(screened),
  citations_results          = nrow(new_fit),
  other_sought_reports       = nrow(new_fit_filtered),
  other_notretrieved_reports = snowball |> filter(decision_ft == "not retrievable") |> nrow(),
  other_assessed             = snowball |> filter(decision_ft != "not retrievable") |> nrow(),
  other_excluded             = reasons_text(snowball),
  new_studies                = n_included + included_snow,
  new_reports                = n_included + included_snow
)
for (box in names(counts)) {
  template <- set_n(template, box, counts[[box]])
}

flow <- PRISMA_data(as.data.frame(template))
diagram <- PRISMA_flowdiagram(flow, previous = FALSE, other = TRUE, fontsize = 12)
prisma_file <- here("output", "prisma.svg")
PRISMA_save(diagram, filename = prisma_file, filetype = "SVG", overwrite = TRUE)
PRISMA_save(diagram, filename = here("output", "prisma.png"),
            filetype = "PNG", overwrite = TRUE)
```

@fig-prisma summarises the fate of every record. Of the `r nrow(works)`
records the string found, `r n_included` are included; snowballing adds
`r included_snow` more, so that the review rests on
`r n_included + included_snow` studies (@tbl-included).

```{r}
#| label: fig-prisma
#| fig-cap: "PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of the example review. The arm on the right counts the records found by snowballing from the two seeds chosen for fit; of those, only the records that passed the title filter were sought for retrieval."
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(prisma_file)
```

`other = TRUE` draws the right-hand arm for snowballing; `previous = FALSE`
hides the arm for earlier versions of a review, which this one does not have.

## The included studies

```{r}
#| label: tbl-included
#| tbl-cap: "The included studies, by route and year."
bind_rows(
  works |>
    filter(id %in% included_db_ids) |>
    transmute(Year = publication_year, Title = title,
              Source = coalesce(source_display_name, "(none)"), Route = "string"),
  new_fit_filtered |>
    filter(id %in% included_snow_ids) |>
    transmute(Year = publication_year, Title = title,
              Source = coalesce(source_display_name, "(none)"), Route = "snowballing")
) |>
  arrange(Year) |>
  nice_table() |>
  width(j = "Title", width = 4) |>
  width(j = "Source", width = 1.6)
```

These are the studies that would enter the concept matrix (step 7 of the
tutorial).
